rail_guard.text: New Street. Trains for every station you have visited in England, Wales and Scotland, plus a few you have only heard of. Mind the gap, mind the step, mind the pigeon wearing a high-vis.

brum_boater_chat.text: Eleven miles an hour on a canal is a speed crime. We do three, and we overtake no one, and we are all very happy.
Lots of Birmingham's canals were built in the 1700s to carry coal and iron. Now they carry tea and tourists. The tea is the better cargo.

then.text: You've had the Birmingham grand tour. More canals than Venice, and fewer gondoliers. We make up for it in kettles.

else.text: The captain pats the tiller. Hop aboard for a trip along the cut?

then.text: Mind your head at the bridges. Mind your tea at the locks. Mind the swan. The swan is an admiral.
The narrowboat slides out under the brick arches at about the speed of a thoughtful snail.
Gas lamps, rusty towpath rings, and a heron on a lock gate who regards your passing as a mild inconvenience. A cyclist overtakes you. Then a duck.
Gas Street Basin. Brindleyplace. The old Roundhouse. There are thirty-five miles of canal inside the city, give or take, and I know every one of them by its smell.
At the end of the trip the captain presses a flask into your hands, still warm.
That's for the road. Fresh brewed, three sugars, and a biscuit for the swan. Come back and I'll show you the Black Country the long way.

else.text: Another time. The canal's not going anywhere. That's rather its whole charm.

then.text: Raining again, bab. Good job the library's got ten floors of dry. I've read three books just waiting for it to stop.
Up at dawn for a nine o'clock lecture. I'm not a morning person. I'm barely an afternoon person.

brum_student.text: {greeting} The Library of Birmingham is the biggest public library in Britain. The shelves go on forever. I got lost looking for the exit and found a better book.
There's a rooftop garden with a view over the whole city. You can see the Bullring, the canals, and, on a clear day, my overdue fines.

then.text: Bit of drizzle, bab. Brum's got more canal than Venice, so a bit more water won't hurt nobody.
Bostin' day, innit? Sun out on the Bullring and everyone's suddenly found their sunglasses.
Lights coming on round the Bullring. Lovely. Tara-a-bit to the daylight, eh?

brum_bull.text: Brummies say 'bab' when they mean 'love' and 'bostin' when they mean 'brilliant'. You'll hear 'tara-a-bit' when someone leaves. It means they'll miss you.
Oh, and 'Brummie' is the word for a person from Birmingham. 'Brum' for the city. 'Brumagem' if you're older than the Rotunda.

brum_baker.text: The Balti was born in Birmingham, in a wok-like pan, in the 1970s. It arrives sizzling and you eat it with naan instead of cutlery. The Balti Triangle has more curry houses per square foot than anywhere sane.
Mild, medium, or hot. Do not say 'hot' to impress anyone. I will remember.

then.text: Fog's in. The departure board says 'delayed'. I'd say 'lost', personally.
Wind's whistling through New Street. My tent's holding up better than my hat.
Last train's gone, has it? Good thing I brought the tent. Platform 12 has a lovely view.

brum_traveller.text: {greeting} Birmingham New Street is the busiest station in Britain outside London. I'm told it has a great deal of rail and a great deal of pigeons.
My train's late. It's alright. I've brought a book. And a pasty. And a tent.

birmingham_fox_watcher.text: Shh. There's a fox on the canal towpath. Brum's foxes know the canals better than the boaters do.
Red torch, see. Foxes don't mind red light, so they carry on being nosy and I get to watch.
Night-time in the city, it's all foxes, owls and the odd person heading home with a balti. Lovely.

birmingham_night_boater.text: Moored up at Gas Street Basin for the night. The water goes all gold under the lamps.
No locks after dark, that's my rule. Brum's got more canal than Venice, and I'm not doing it in the dark.
